mcq.prompt: Which three parts does every asynchronous mechanism in this chapter have?
choices: A thread, a mutex, and a condition variable
A callback, an event loop, and a work queue
A task, shared state that records completion and holds the outcome, and a result channel to the consumer
A coroutine frame, a promise type, and an awaiter
mcq.explain: Task, shared state, result channel — the triple survives every packaging in the chapter, from promise/future to coroutines to senders. The thread/mutex/condition-variable answer names one possible implementation of the shared state rather than the structure, and the coroutine answer names the parts of exactly one mechanism. Recognising the triple is what lets you compare mechanisms on ownership, error channel, cancellation, and cost.

mcq.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the three costs the chapter attributes to callback-based sequencing?
choices: Callbacks are inherently slower than futures, because each invocation allocates
Inversion of control — the event loop, not the visible function body, decides when each continuation runs
Error plumbing — an exception cannot cross an event-loop turn, so every callback needs an explicit failure path
Callback nesting — each dependent operation introduces another lambda and another lifetime boundary
mcq.explain: The three costs are all about structure, not speed. Callbacks are in fact the cheapest option on the allocation axis: with fixed storage a callback pipeline can be allocation-free, whereas a future mandates a separately allocated shared state. That is exactly why the chapter's verdict table calls callbacks 'viable if tightly controlled' — you give up composability and error propagation, not performance.

mcq.prompt: A registered completion callback captures a local variable by reference. What is the rule?
choices: It is safe, because the event loop copies the captured state when it stores the callback
It is safe as long as the callback is eventually invoked on the thread that registered it
It is safe if the local is const, since nothing can modify it after the function returns
It is a dangling capture — a callback often outlives the function that registered it, so capture owned state by value or place it in an object whose lifetime covers the operation
mcq.explain: Registering a callback is the moment the operation's lifetime stops matching the registering function's scope; the loop invokes it on some later turn, after that stack frame is gone. Nothing copies the referred-to object — the closure stores a reference, and const changes access, not lifetime. Running on the same thread does not help either, because the problem is *when* it runs, not *where*.

mcq.prompt: `result.get()` is called a second time on a `std::future<double>` whose first get() already returned. What happens?
choices: It returns the same value again, since the shared state still holds it
It throws std::future_error, because the first get() moved the result out and left the future with no associated state
It blocks forever waiting for a second value
The behaviour is undefined
mcq.explain: get() is a one-shot transfer: it waits, moves the result out, and invalidates the future, after which valid() is false and any further operation throws std::future_error. Waiting does not consume the state — only get() does. If several consumers must observe the same result, that is what std::shared_future is for; its get() leaves the state readable.

mcq.prompt: What does `std::shared_future<T>` change relative to `std::future<T>`?
choices: It allows set_value() to be called more than once on the associated promise
It removes the separately allocated shared state
Its get() does not consume the state, so several consumers may wait on and read the same result
It makes the producer end copyable so several threads can fulfil it
mcq.explain: shared_future changes only the consumer end: many observers, non-consuming get(). The producer side is unchanged — a shared state still has exactly one producer slot, so a second set_value() throws either way. It also does not save an allocation; if anything it extends the shared state's lifetime, since the state must survive until the last shared_future is gone.

mcq.prompt: A worker running behind a promise throws. How does the exception reach the consumer?
choices: The worker catches it and stores it with set_exception(); get() rethrows it in the consumer, preserving the exception type
The runtime propagates it across the thread boundary automatically when the thread exits
It calls std::terminate — exceptions cannot cross a thread boundary at all
get() returns a value-initialized result and sets an error flag the consumer must check
mcq.explain: Exceptions do not propagate between threads on their own — an exception escaping a thread's top-level function calls std::terminate. The future's result channel is what makes propagation possible: the worker captures the active exception with std::current_exception() and stores it, and get() rethrows the stored std::exception_ptr in the consumer, so the consumer's catch clauses match the original type. The terminate answer is right about raw threads and wrong about this mechanism.

mcq.prompt: A `std::promise<int>` is destroyed without ever calling set_value() or set_exception(). What does a waiting consumer's get() do?
choices: Blocks forever, since the shared state never becomes ready
Returns a value-initialized int
Calls std::terminate
Throws std::future_error carrying the broken_promise condition
mcq.explain: The promise's destructor makes the shared state ready with a broken_promise error rather than leaving a consumer parked forever — a deliberate 'the producer disappeared' signal. What it cannot tell you is *why* it disappeared, which is why a worker should still catch its own failures and store the original exception; broken_promise should be reserved for genuinely abandoned work.

mcq.prompt: A `std::packaged_task` that has already run to completion is invoked a second time. What happens?
choices: It runs again and overwrites the stored result
It throws std::future_error, because its shared state already has a result and a shared state has one producer slot
It silently does nothing and the future keeps the first result
It creates a second shared state, which the original future does not see
mcq.explain: A packaged_task is one-shot with respect to its current shared state: invoking it again attempts to publish a second result and throws, exactly as calling set_value() twice on a promise would. (Invoking a default-constructed or moved-from task throws too, reporting no state.) This is why a task queue must treat each wrapper as one consumable work item rather than a reusable function object.

mcq.prompt: In the chapter's `submit()`, why is the `std::packaged_task` wrapped in a `std::shared_ptr` before being enqueued?
choices: So that several workers can run the same task concurrently
Because std::packaged_task is not safe to invoke from a pool worker
Because the pool's std::function<void()> queue accepts only copyable callables, and a packaged_task is move-only
To keep the future's shared state alive after the task completes
mcq.explain: std::function requires a copy-constructible target, and packaged_task is move-only — so the shared_ptr exists purely to make a move-only object reachable through a copyable handle. The extra owner and its control-block allocation are an adaptation to the old queue type, not something intrinsic to packaged_task: switching the queue to std::move_only_function<void()> lets a lambda capture the task directly and removes it. The future's shared state is reference-managed independently and needs no help.

mcq.prompt: A future returned by `std::async` with the default policy keeps returning `std::future_status::deferred` from wait_for(). What must the caller do to make progress?
choices: Call get(), or perform a non-timed wait — a deferred callable never runs merely because wait_for() is polled
Keep polling; the implementation will schedule the work once a worker becomes free
Call wait_until() with a longer deadline, so the runtime has time to start the thread
Discard the future and reconstruct it with std::launch::async
mcq.explain: std::launch::deferred is lazy synchronous execution, not background work — there is no thread waiting to be scheduled. The callable runs on the waiting thread, and only a non-timed wait or get() triggers it, so a polling loop written for an async future spins forever on a deferred one. This is the concrete reason to write the launch policy explicitly whenever the behaviour matters: with the default policy either shape is permitted.

mcq.prompt: Two consecutive statements each call `std::async(std::launch::async, work)` and discard the returned future. What is the observed behaviour?
choices: Both run concurrently on two new threads
Neither runs — discarding the future cancels the work before it starts
Both are silently downgraded to deferred and never run at all
They serialize: each temporary future's destructor waits for its shared state, so the second call does not start until the first has finished
mcq.explain: A special rule makes a future returned by std::async wait in its destructor when it is the last reference to an unfinished asynchronous shared state — and a discarded return value is a temporary destroyed at the end of its full-expression. So each statement blocks until its own work completes, and code that looks like fan-out is fully sequential. The work is neither cancelled nor skipped; storing the futures in named variables is what actually keeps both operations outstanding.

mcq.prompt: According to the chapter's latency summary, which cost is intrinsic to a promise/future pair?
choices: Every get() creates a thread to perform the wait
A separately allocated, reference-managed shared state, plus a blocking rendezvous in get()
One allocation per waiting consumer
A kernel transition on every set_value()
mcq.explain: The shared state is where the result and the readiness flag live, so a future cannot express its result channel without one — normally a separate allocation managed much like a shared_ptr control block. Combined with get() being a blocking rendezvous, that is the reason the chapter keeps futures off a tick path. Contrast senders: a pipeline can stay an inert, allocation-free description until it is connected and started.

mcq.prompt: Why does C++ provide no operation that preemptively kills a running thread?
choices: Because no mainstream operating system exposes such an operation
Because it would be an ABI break for existing implementations
Because stopping code at an arbitrary point could strand a held mutex, leave an invariant half-updated, or leak an external resource
Because std::jthread already provides it through its destructor
mcq.explain: The objection is a correctness one, not a portability one: there is no safe arbitrary point at which to stop a thread, because the victim may be holding a lock or midway through restoring an invariant. So cancellation is cooperative — a component requests a stop and the worker observes it at a point it has chosen. jthread's destructor requests exactly that kind of stop and then joins; it has no power to interrupt a worker that never checks.

mcq.prompt: A `std::stop_callback` is constructed on a token whose stop has already been requested. What happens?
choices: The callback is invoked during registration, closing the race between checking the token and installing the hook
Registration throws, because the stop state is already final
The callback is never invoked, since the request it would have observed has passed
The callback is queued and invoked at the next request_stop()
mcq.explain: Without that rule, code that tests the token and then registers a wake hook would lose any request landing between the two steps — and there is no way to close that window from the outside. Inline invocation on registration removes it. The consequence is that the callback may run either on the requesting thread or on the registering thread, so it must be short and safe in both contexts. Note also that a stop request is permanent: there is no reset, so a later request_stop() returns false and invokes nothing.

mcq.prompt: An I/O completion, a stop request, and a deadline can all fire at nearly the same moment for one operation. What is the correct structure?
choices: Test a Boolean before registering the callbacks, so that only one of them can ever be armed
One atomic compare-exchange — or one executor-confined transition — claims the terminal state; the winner publishes the result and resumes the consumer, and the losers only clean up
Give each event its own flag and let the consumer read all three when it wakes
Take a mutex in each callback and let whichever acquires it last decide
mcq.explain: There are three contenders and exactly one terminal result, so the design question is who gets to claim it. A single compare_exchange from `pending` to a terminal value answers that: precisely one caller sees true, publishes, and schedules the continuation once. Testing a Boolean before registering does not work — cancellation can arrive between the test and the registration, which is the very window std::stop_callback's inline invocation exists to close. Letting the last mutex holder decide permits two resumptions of the same consumer.

mcq.prompt: What makes a C++ function a coroutine?
choices: Declaring its return type to be a type that has a nested promise_type
Annotating it with a `coroutine` specifier
Its body containing co_await, co_yield, or co_return
Returning std::future or std::generator
mcq.explain: It is a property of the body, not the declaration: one of the three keywords anywhere in the body makes the compiler transform the function into a resumable state machine. The return type matters only afterwards — it must select a promise_type, and a body with co_return and a return type of `int` is ill-formed for exactly that reason. Note the consequence for interfaces: whether a function is a coroutine is invisible at its declaration.

mcq.prompt: A `co_await` suspends a coroutine. What does that imply about threads?
choices: The current thread blocks until the awaited operation completes
A new thread is created to carry the rest of the coroutine
The coroutine is guaranteed to resume on the thread that suspended it
Nothing: control returns to the caller or scheduler, and whichever component calls resume() determines the thread the body continues on
mcq.explain: Suspension is a control-flow operation on a state machine, not a thread operation — the point of it is precisely that the thread is released to do other work instead of blocking. It equally does not create a thread. And it makes no affinity promise: a reactor thread or a pool worker may call resume(), so a coroutine can start on one thread and continue on another. That is why thread-local state and lock ownership must not be assumed to survive a suspension.

mcq.prompt: Which coroutine parameters are owned by the coroutine frame?
choices: All of them — the frame copies every parameter so that it can outlive the caller
Value parameters become values owned by the frame; reference parameters remain references, so their external lifetime becomes part of the coroutine's contract
None — parameters stay in the caller's stack frame and are read through it
Only the parameters that are still live after the first suspension point
mcq.explain: The frame stores parameters, but storing a reference parameter stores a reference, not a copy of what it names. Since a coroutine can suspend and resume long after its caller's expression has finished, a reference parameter bound to a temporary or a caller local is a dangling read waiting to happen — and it is silent, because the frame's copy of the reference is perfectly valid. Prefer by-value parameters for coroutines, or document the lifetime requirement explicitly.

mcq.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
mcq.prompt: The chapter's Task returns `std::suspend_always` from `final_suspend()`. What breaks if it returns `std::suspend_never` instead?
choices: The coroutine body never runs, because the frame is destroyed before initial_suspend
co_return stops routing through return_value(), so the result is never stored
The frame destroys itself at completion, leaving the owning Task's handle dangling and its stored result unreadable
unhandled_exception() is no longer called for an escaping exception
mcq.explain: final_suspend is the hook that keeps a completed frame alive so its owner can observe the result before calling destroy(). Returning suspend_never lets the frame release itself immediately at completion — after which Task::get() reads the promise through a handle into freed storage, and Task's destructor calls destroy() on it a second time. The result *is* stored via return_value() before final_suspend runs; the bug is purely that nothing is left to read it from. (final_suspend must also be noexcept.)

mcq.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
mcq.prompt: Which awaiter operation supplies the value of the `co_await` expression?
choices: await_resume()
await_ready()
await_suspend()
get_return_object(), on the promise
mcq.explain: The triple divides the work: await_ready() answers 'can we continue without suspending?', await_suspend() answers 'who stores or resumes this coroutine?', and await_resume() answers 'what is this expression's value?'. await_resume() is called on both paths — after a real suspension and when await_ready() returned true — which is what makes the fast path and the suspended path yield the same expression. get_return_object() belongs to the promise and produces the caller's handle, not the co_await result.

mcq.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
mcq.prompt: `await_suspend()` may return void, bool, or a `std::coroutine_handle`. What does returning a handle mean?
choices: The suspension is cancelled and the awaiting coroutine continues immediately
That handle's frame is destroyed as part of the suspension
The handle is stored for the caller to resume manually later
Symmetric transfer — execution resumes that coroutine directly, without growing the ordinary call stack
mcq.explain: Returning void commits to the suspension; returning false from the bool form is what cancels it. Returning a handle means 'suspend me and continue in this other coroutine', and the transfer is a tail call rather than a nested resume(), so a chain of coroutines resuming each other cannot overflow the stack. Production Task types use it to hop from a completing child straight into its parent's continuation.

mcq.prompt: How many allocations does iterating a `std::generator<Tick>` over N inputs normally require?
choices: One per yielded element, since each suspension stores a new value
Normally one — for the coroutine frame — unless the compiler applies allocation elision
None: generator frames are always placed in the caller's stack frame
One for the frame plus one for the internal vector that buffers the results
mcq.explain: A generator is one coroutine, so it has one frame, and the range-for machinery just resumes that same frame repeatedly. Nothing is buffered: no std::vector<Tick> is built, which is precisely why breaking out of the loop early decodes only the ticks actually consumed. Elision (HALO) may remove even that one allocation when the compiler can prove the frame's lifetime nests within the caller — but it is an optimization to verify in generated code, not a guarantee.

mcq.prompt: A loop holds on to a reference obtained from a `std::generator` and then advances the iterator. What is the risk?
choices: None — yielded values remain valid for the generator's whole lifetime
The generator restarts from the beginning, because it is single-pass
Incrementing resumes the producer, which may overwrite the storage used for the previous yielded value — copy it before advancing if it must survive
The reference silently acquires const qualification after the increment
mcq.explain: std::generator is move-only and single-pass, and advancing means resuming the producer coroutine. A value yielded from a loop-local object lives only as long as that object does — often only until the next resume — so a reference kept across an increment can dangle. The fix is to copy before advancing. 'Restarts from the beginning' is a different misconception: single-pass means the sequence cannot be traversed twice at all, not that it rewinds.

mcq.prompt: After `auto work = std::execution::then(std::execution::schedule(scheduler), compute);` completes, what has happened?
choices: Nothing has been scheduled — a sender is an inert description of work until it is connected and started
compute() has already been queued to and run on the scheduler's execution context
A thread has been created and is blocked waiting for the pipeline to be started
A shared state has been allocated and marked pending
mcq.explain: The sender expression builds a description as an ordinary value. Work begins only when connecting a sender to a receiver produces an operation state and something starts it — directly, or through an algorithm such as sync_wait. That laziness is the model's advantage over a future: a future's shared state must exist because the result channel needs somewhere to live, whereas a sender pipeline can stay allocation-free until start.

mcq.prompt: Where does the chapter place coroutines relative to a hot tick-to-trade loop?
choices: They are the preferred hot-path abstraction, since an awaiter can return true from await_ready()
They are equivalent to callbacks in cost, so the choice is a matter of style
They should replace the thread pool entirely, since one parked frame is cheaper than one blocked thread
Usually the wrong shape: frame allocation must be eliminated or pooled, resume uses an indirect control transfer, and the body splits across resume points in the instruction cache
mcq.explain: Coroutines earn their place in orchestration — connection logic, startup sequencing, administration — where an outstanding operation waits far more than it computes, and where one parked frame genuinely replaces one blocked thread and stack. On a tick loop the three named costs all land at once. The await_ready() answer is the specific trap the chapter warns about: an awaiter that always reports ready benchmarks the synchronous fast path and measures none of the suspension, registration, and resumption cost you are actually buying.

reading.explain: 4 + 9 + 1 = 14, and the default ostream formatting prints a whole-valued double as '14'. The result is deterministic despite the thread because get() is a rendezvous: it blocks until the shared state is ready, so no scheduling order can change what is printed. Note the move capture — std::promise is move-only, so the producer end is transferred into the closure while the consumer keeps the future.

It prints 'broken'. The promise's destructor does not simply abandon the shared state: it makes it ready with a broken_promise error, so get() throws std::future_error rather than blocking forever. That is the useful part of the design — a consumer always learns that the producer disappeared. What it does not learn is why, which is why every producer path should still fulfil its promise deliberately and let broken_promise mean genuinely abandoned work.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The capture `[promise = producer]` copy-initialises from a std::promise, and std::promise is move-only — its copy constructor is deleted, so the program is ill-formed. That refusal is the type system enforcing the model: a shared state has exactly one producer slot, so there is no meaningful way for two threads to hold the same producer end. If several threads must be able to complete the operation, the right shape is one owner plus an explicit terminal-state arbitration.

Invoking the packaged_task runs the callable on the calling thread — nothing here is asynchronous — and routes the return value into the shared state, so get() yields 42. The second invocation tries to publish a second result into a state that already has one and throws std::future_error. A packaged_task is one-shot with respect to its shared state, not a reusable function object, which is why a task queue must treat each wrapper as a single consumable work item.

Three separate rules, all visible in one line of output. The token starts unrequested; request_stop() sets the state permanently. The stop_callback is then registered on an already-requested token, so it is invoked inline *during construction* — that is the rule that closes the race between testing a token and installing a wake hook. Finally, a stop state cannot be requested twice: the second request_stop() changes nothing, invokes nothing, and returns false. This program is single-threaded, so none of it depends on scheduling.

reading.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
reading.explain: await_suspend() is never called. await_ready() returns true, so the co_await takes the synchronous fast path straight to await_resume(), which supplies the expression's value — this is the whole mechanism behind an awaiter that already has its result cached. initial_suspend() returning suspend_never means the body runs eagerly during the call, and final_suspend() returning suspend_always keeps the completed frame alive so result() can read the promise before ~Task destroys it. Note what an always-ready awaiter costs you as a benchmark: it measures none of the suspension, registration, and resumption work that a real I/O awaiter performs.

reading.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: A coroutine handle is a non-owning access path to a frame, not an owner — destroy() releases the frame's storage but leaves `task.handle` holding the same address, still contextually convertible to true. Resuming it reads the destroyed frame's resume pointer, which is undefined behaviour; AddressSanitizer reports 'heap-use-after-free ... READ of size 8', because the frame came from an allocation function. The rule is unconditional: never resume a completed or destroyed frame. The same hazard is why a cancellation-aware awaiter must detach every I/O, timer, and stop registration that could reach the handle before the frame is destroyed.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: The co_return in the body makes this a coroutine, and the compiler then looks up std::coroutine_traits<int>::promise_type to find the policy object for the frame. There is no such member for `int`, so the program is ill-formed — clang says as much: "this function cannot be a coroutine: 'std::coroutine_traits<int>' has no member named 'promise_type'". The lesson is the direction of the dependency: the keyword in the body is what makes it a coroutine, and the return type is then obliged to supply the machinery.

writing.prompt: A function builds a request, registers a completion callback with an event loop, and returns. The callback needs the request's correlation id and its symbol. Write a version whose captured state cannot dangle, and add a comment naming the defect in the by-reference version.
checklist: The callback captures owned state by value (or owns it through a shared state object), never by reference to a local
A comment states that the callback runs on a later event-loop turn, after the registering frame is gone
The failure path is handled explicitly inside the callback, not by letting an exception escape
Nothing captured refers to a parameter passed by reference to the registering function
writing.notes: The rule is that registering a callback is the point where the operation's lifetime stops matching the registering function's scope, so every piece of state the callback touches needs an owner that outlives the operation. Note that taking `symbol` by value in the signature is what makes the move capture cheap — the caller decides whether to copy or move, and the closure ends up owning it either way.

writing.prompt: Write a worker function that computes a risk number and publishes it through a `std::promise<double>`. It must fulfil the promise on every path, including when the computation throws, and the consumer's catch must see the original exception type. Then show the consumer side.
checklist: The promise is moved into the worker, not copied (std::promise is move-only)
The success path calls set_value() exactly once
A catch(...) block stores std::current_exception() with set_exception()
No path can leave the promise unfulfilled other than genuine abandonment
The consumer wraps get() in a try/catch that names the original exception type
writing.notes: Note the shape of the try: only the call that can throw is inside it, and set_value() is invoked with the already-computed result, so a throwing computation cannot leave a half-set state. Letting the promise's destructor produce broken_promise instead is a strictly worse error report — it tells the consumer that the producer disappeared but discards the reason.

writing.prompt: Add a `submit()` to Chapter 23's thread pool that returns a `std::future` for the callable's result, given that the pool's queue holds `std::function<void()>`. Explain in a comment which part of your solution is an adaptation to that queue type rather than intrinsic to packaged_task.
checklist: Wraps the callable in a std::packaged_task whose signature matches the deduced result type
Obtains the future from the packaged_task before enqueuing it
Uses std::make_shared so the move-only task is reachable from a copyable std::function
Uses std::invoke_result_t (or equivalent) rather than a fixed result type
A comment states that std::move_only_function<void()> removes the shared_ptr
Returns the future to the caller, not the packaged_task
writing.notes: Invoking the packaged_task routes a returned value or a thrown exception into the shared state automatically, so the worker needs no try/catch — that is the feature packaged_task adds over a bare callable. Take care that each queued wrapper is consumed exactly once: a second invocation would try to publish a second result and throw std::future_error.

writing.prompt: Write a consumer that waits for a message on a condition variable and returns promptly when a stop is requested. Write it twice: once with a plain `std::condition_variable` plus an explicit `std::stop_callback`, and once with the `std::condition_variable_any` stop-token overload. Comment on what makes the first version race-free.
checklist: The stop_callback version registers the hook before the wait begins
Its predicate tests both the message state and stop.stop_requested()
A comment states that registering on an already-requested token invokes the callback inline, closing the check-then-register race
The condition_variable_any version uses the three-argument wait and checks its bool result
Both versions read and modify predicate state only while holding the mutex
A comment notes that plain std::condition_variable has no stop-token overload
writing.notes: The predicate in the first version has to include stop_requested() even with the callback installed: the notification only wakes the waiter, and a woken waiter that rechecks a predicate mentioning nothing about stopping goes straight back to sleep. Cancellation latency is bounded by how often the worker reaches a check and whether its blocking operations can be woken at all — wiring the wake hook is what turns the request into a prompt return rather than an eventual one.

writing.prompt: An asynchronous operation can be completed by its I/O callback, cancelled by a stop request, or abandoned by a deadline. Write the state object that lets exactly one of the three claim the terminal result, and comment on what a losing caller must and must not do.
checklist: A single std::atomic holding an enumerated state, initialised to a pending value
One compare_exchange from pending to the terminal value, shared by all three entry points
The claim function returns bool so only the winner publishes and resumes
compare_exchange_strong is used with an acquire/release success ordering
A comment states that losers release their own registrations but must not resume the consumer again
writing.notes: compare_exchange_strong is right here because there is no retry loop to absorb a spurious failure — a single attempt has to be conclusive. The acquire/release pair orders the terminal-state publication against the result the winner writes. A runtime that confines all three callbacks to one executor can drop the atomic entirely and serialize the decision through the executor instead. And note the residual hazard the state object does not solve: a timeout result does not prove the underlying I/O stopped, so the implementation must still cancel and drain it or keep the callback state alive until a late completion is harmlessly consumed.

writing.prompt: Given a gateway whose connect, send and confirm operations each return an awaitable Task, rewrite the three-level nested callback submission as a coroutine. Then state in a comment which of the three callback costs the rewrite removes and which lifetime obligation it introduces.
checklist: The body is straight-line: three co_awaits and a co_return, no nesting
The connection obtained from the first await is used by the later operations as an ordinary local
Order parameters are taken by value, not by reference
A comment names inversion of control, error plumbing, and callback nesting as what the rewrite addresses
A comment states that a reference parameter would stay a reference in the frame and must outlive every suspension
writing.notes: `connection` is a local that must survive two suspensions, so it lives in the frame; a local used only between two awaits may stay in a register or vanish under optimization. Note that `gateway` is deliberately a reference here — that is a real contract, not an oversight: the gateway must outlive the whole session, which is precisely the kind of requirement structured concurrency exists to make checkable.

writing.section: The promise type, awaiters, and the frame
writing.prompt: Write an Event that a coroutine can co_await: awaiting it continues immediately if the event is already set, and otherwise parks the coroutine until another component calls set(). Implement the awaiter triple explicitly and comment on why await_suspend returns bool here.
checklist: await_ready() returns true when the event is already set, skipping suspension entirely
await_suspend() stores the coroutine handle and returns bool
await_suspend() re-checks the set flag and returns false to cancel the suspension if it lost the race
await_resume() supplies the co_await expression's value
set() resumes the stored handle, and clears it first so it cannot be resumed twice
A comment explains that returning false from await_suspend cancels the suspension
writing.notes: This is the shape of every real I/O awaiter: await_ready() reports whether the result is already available, await_suspend() registers the handle with whatever will complete the operation, and await_resume() produces the value. The third return form — another std::coroutine_handle — performs symmetric transfer, resuming that coroutine as a tail call so a chain of continuations cannot grow the stack. Note the ownership rule underneath all of it: the handle is a non-owning access path, so set() must not run after the frame has been destroyed.

writing.prompt: Your toolchain's standard library does not yet ship <generator>. Write a minimal move-only Generator<T> with the promise_type, iterator and sentinel needed for a range-for loop, and use it to write a lazy sequence with co_yield. Note in a comment how many allocations iterating it performs.
checklist: promise_type provides yield_value() returning std::suspend_always
initial_suspend() returns std::suspend_always so nothing runs before the first increment
The type is move-only and destroys the frame in its destructor
begin() resumes once to produce the first element; end() returns a sentinel compared against done()
An escaping exception is captured by unhandled_exception() and rethrown to the consumer
A comment states one frame allocation for the whole sequence, none per element
writing.notes: yield_value() is what co_yield routes through: it stores the element in the promise and returns an awaiter, and returning suspend_always is what makes the sequence lazy. Note the consequence for the consumer — the yielded value lives in the promise and is overwritten on the next resume, so a reference held across an increment dangles. That is the same single-pass, copy-before-advancing contract std::generator has, and it is why the type is move-only.
